Stage kernels run on preallocated buffers; e2e methods allocate per call.

part_b.design: random-init BF16 weights, random tokens; NVFP4 variants replace every block linear (qkv, out, gate, up, down) by an RTN NVFP4Linear with dynamic activation scales. Embedding, RMSNorms, attention (SDPA) and the tied LM head stay BF16. `_graph`: one CUDA graph per forward. bf16_compiled: torch.compile default mode.

caveats: Part A/B weights and activations are random; latency does not depend on values. Part C uses a real 320-step single-seed 50m checkpoint, so W4A4 deltas are for one small, briefly trained model.
Dynamic activation scales cost a second read of the activation (amax pass); the static path skips it but saturates activations above the train.bin calibration maximum.
Static scales are calibrated on the BF16 model's activations, not on the upstream-quantized model.
Under autocast, NVFP4Linear quantizes whatever dtype reaches it (FP32 or BF16) directly; the W4A16 reference casts activations to BF16 and weights (dequantized FP32) to BF16 before the GEMM.
bf16_compiled is torch.compile(default); NVFP4 models run eager or as CUDA graphs, not compiled.
CUDA-event resolution on this GPU is about 2 us, so single-call sub-10-us numbers are averages of quantized samples (mean over iters per round, median over rounds).
Isolated Part A stage kernels run cold on preallocated buffers, so the sum of stage medians is a micro-benchmark breakdown rather than an additive model of end-to-end call time.
NVFP4 e2e (had_b16, CUDA graph) is slower than BF16 cuBLAS at (1024,512,1408): activation quantization and the FP4 GEMM do not amortize at these sizes.
